title: The Threshold Theorem in Watts: Fault Tolerance as a Question About Objective Probability
abstract: In 2011 Hagar & Sergioli proposed a new interpretation of objective probability in deterministic physics. On it, the probability of a physical state supervenes on the resources, energy over time, required to realize it from a given state, relative to the resources available (arXiv:1101.3521). The motivation for that paper was an objective alternative to QBism, the view that sees quantum probabilities as subjective degrees of belief. Here I apply this interpretation to a more practical subject matter: fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Under the resource-bounded measure Hagar & Sergioli proposed, the threshold theorem becomes a claim about classification: it asserts that error-corrected logical states belong to the class of relatively cheaply realizable states, whose probability remains near 1 as the machine grows. The theorem originally derived this claim from a resource inventory that was partial, and left out four resources consumed by error correction: calibration of a drifting device, decoding within the correction cycle, coherence as a finite time budget, and entropy flush through fresh ancillas. These entered the original derivation at zero price. Here I translate the feasibility of FTQC into a measurable quantity, watts per decade of suppressed logical error (a decade, in the engineer's usage, being one factor of ten in the error rate). I then show that the published record already contains its first data points for this translation, and I state the two measurements that would settle the question empirically. The three-decade debate on FTQC, conducted so far as an exchange about noise-model assumptions, turns out to be, under this interpretation, a quantitative dispute about a single object: the resource-bounded objective probability of the target logical states.
summary: This paper reframes the Threshold Theorem for fault-tolerant quantum computing by applying an objective probability measure based on resource costs (like energy). The authors argue that standard analyses neglect crucial overheads such as calibration and decoding power. By quantifying these missing resources in watts, they transform a theoretical debate into a concrete, measurable engineering challenge.
main_problem: The paper reinterprets the Threshold Theorem for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) by framing it as a question of objective resource probability rather than just circuit combinatorics.
main_result: By incorporating previously unpriced overheads like calibration, decoding latency, and entropy flushing, the required resources to maintain logical coherence are quantified in watts per decade of error suppression.
method: The authors translate FTQC feasibility into a measurable resource cost (watts/decade) using a novel objective probability measure derived from Hagar & Sergioli's work.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation, specifically concerning the scaling of error correction overheads for logical qubits.
key_observables: Watts per decade of suppressed logical error; resource cost curves comparing quantum vs. classical computation.
important_parameters: Logical error rate ($\epsilon$); machine size (number of physical qubits/distance); power budget (watts).
main_assumptions: The interpretation relies on deterministic dynamics and the assumption that all necessary resources (calibration, decoding, etc.) must be accounted for in the objective probability measure.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the resource-bounded objective probability framework. It then applies this to FTQC, identifying four previously unpriced overheads. Finally, it translates the theoretical threshold into a concrete measurement: watts per decade of error suppression.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful physical lens—resource accounting—to re-evaluate fundamental computational complexity results in quantum information theory, connecting abstract theorems to measurable engineering constraints.
